ctx: Tensions between France and Prussia were already high over a Prussian prince's candidacy for the vacant Spanish throne, which France saw as a strategic encirclement threat. Bismarck was looking for a pretext to unite the still-separate German states behind Prussia through a war against a common enemy.
fa: Bismarck edited a routine diplomatic telegram to make a polite exchange between the Prussian king and the French ambassador sound like a mutual insult, then released it to the press. France declared war within six days, giving Bismarck the conflict he wanted to unify Germany under Prussian leadership.

ctx: By early 1917, the United States had stayed officially neutral in World War I for over two years despite German submarine attacks sinking ships carrying American citizens. Germany anticipated that resuming unrestricted submarine warfare would likely draw the US into the war and wanted a way to keep America distracted on its own continent.
fa: German foreign secretary Arthur Zimmermann secretly proposed a military alliance with Mexico against the United States, offering to help Mexico reclaim Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. British codebreakers intercepted and decoded the message, and its publication helped push a reluctant United States into the war.

n: The secret protocol of the Nazi-Soviet Pact
ctx: A week before Germany invaded Poland, the two ideological enemies of Nazism and Communism stunned the world by signing a public non-aggression treaty. The publicly announced pact alone was already a diplomatic bombshell, but its hidden territorial arrangement went much further than anyone outside the two governments knew.
fa: Alongside the public treaty, Germany and the Soviet Union signed a secret protocol carving up Poland and the Baltic states into spheres of influence. The Soviet government denied the protocol's existence for decades, even though a German copy had already surfaced in the West after the war; the USSR itself only admitted it was genuine in 1989-1992.

ctx: Eisenhower and Khrushchev had met at Camp David the previous year in a rare moment of Cold War thaw, and a four-power summit in Paris was scheduled to build on that progress just two weeks after the plane went down.
fa: When a Soviet missile shot down an American U-2 spy plane deep inside Soviet territory, Washington's cover story, a weather research flight blown off course, collapsed within days once Moscow revealed it had captured the pilot alive along with his espionage camera. The scandal wrecked the planned summit and froze Cold War relations for years.

n: The secret plan behind the Suez Crisis
ctx: Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser had just nationalized the Suez Canal Company after Western powers withdrew funding for the Aswan Dam, threatening British and French control over a canal vital to their oil supplies and trade routes.
fa: Britain, France, and Israel secretly agreed that Israel would invade Egypt so Britain and France could then step in as supposedly neutral peacekeepers and seize the canal. The plan worked militarily but collapsed diplomatically once the United States found out, and Britain's prime minister spent years publicly denying the collusion had ever happened.

n: How the United States got the Panama Canal
ctx: The United States wanted to build a canal across the isthmus, but Colombia's senate had just rejected the treaty granting the rights, after years of negotiation over compensation terms Colombia considered unfair.
fa: A convenient uprising in the Panamanian province declared independence days later, with American warships standing by to block Colombian troops from intervening. Washington recognized the new nation of Panama almost immediately and had its canal treaty signed before the month was out.

ctx: Britain's first ever Labour government, formed only months earlier, had just recognized the Soviet Union diplomatically and negotiated a trade treaty with it, a move deeply unpopular with conservative and anti-communist factions ahead of the coming election.
fa: Four days before the election, a newspaper published a letter supposedly from a top Soviet official urging British communists toward insurrection. The letter helped sink the governing Labour Party at the polls, and it later turned out to be a forgery, most likely manufactured by anti-Soviet exiles and passed along by sympathetic elements of British intelligence.

n: The fabricated second Gulf of Tonkin attack
ctx: The Johnson administration was looking for congressional authorization to escalate American involvement in Vietnam without a formal declaration of war, at a time when US forces were still officially limited to an advisory role.
fa: The United States told Congress that North Vietnamese boats had attacked American destroyers twice in the Gulf of Tonkin, using the incidents to pass a resolution that opened the door to full-scale war. Declassified documents released decades later confirmed the second attack never happened at all, and that officials knew the evidence was shaky at the time.

n: France bombs a Greenpeace ship in a foreign harbor
ctx: France was in the middle of its nuclear weapons testing program in the South Pacific at Mururoa Atoll, a program facing growing international criticism, and Greenpeace's ship was preparing to lead a flotilla protest against the next scheduled test.
fa: French secret service divers attached mines to the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in a New Zealand harbor to stop the protest, killing a photographer aboard. France denied any involvement for over two months before its prime minister admitted on live television that the government had ordered the attack.

ctx: The US had no formal diplomatic relations with Iran since the 1979 hostage crisis and had publicly imposed an arms embargo on the country, while a separate law banned military aid to Nicaragua's Contra rebels fighting the leftist Sandinista government.
fa: The Reagan administration secretly sold weapons to Iran in a bid to free American hostages, then illegally funneled the profits to fund the Contras. The scheme only came to light after a Lebanese magazine broke the story, triggering a major congressional investigation.

ctx: The Soviet Union had invaded eastern Poland in 1940 under the terms of its pact with Germany and captured thousands of Polish army officers and members of the educated elite as prisoners of war.
fa: The Soviet secret police secretly executed over 22,000 Polish officers and intellectuals in the Katyn forest and elsewhere; when Nazi Germany discovered the mass graves in 1943 and accused the Soviets, Moscow blamed the massacre on the Germans instead, a lie it maintained until finally admitting responsibility in 1990.

ctx: Britain and France were racing to link up their separate African colonial empires along competing north-south and east-west axes, and the headwaters of the Nile in Sudan sat exactly where their ambitions collided.
fa: A small French garrison that had trekked across Africa to plant its flag at Fashoda found itself facing a much larger British force under General Kitchener; both sides raised their flags side by side for weeks while Paris and London edged toward war, until France backed down and withdrew.

ctx: France had just sent troops into the interior of Morocco to put down a rebellion, effectively extending its control over the country in violation of earlier agreements guaranteeing Moroccan independence.
fa: Germany sent a gunboat to the Moroccan port of Agadir, officially to protect German citizens but really to intimidate France into offering compensation elsewhere in Africa. The crisis nearly triggered a European war before it was settled by handing Germany a slice of French Congo.

ctx: Britain had declared neutrality in the American Civil War, but two Confederate diplomats were sailing to Europe to seek British recognition and support for the Southern cause.
fa: A US Navy captain boarded the British mail ship Trent on his own initiative and seized the two Confederate envoys without orders. Britain considered it an act of war and began moving troops toward Canada until President Lincoln quietly released the prisoners to defuse the crisis.

ctx: At the height of the Cold War, any personal connection between a British government minister and a Soviet official carried the risk of compromising national secrets, however incidental the actual link.
fa: Britain's Secretary of State for War lied to Parliament about an affair with a young model who was also involved with a Soviet naval attache suspected of espionage. His forced resignation once the lie was exposed badly damaged the government and contributed to its defeat at the next election.

ctx: Litvinenko was a former Russian intelligence officer who had defected to Britain and become an outspoken critic of the Kremlin, working with Western intelligence services on Russian organized crime.
fa: Litvinenko was poisoned with radioactive polonium-210 slipped into his tea in a London hotel and died three weeks later. A British public inquiry concluded in 2016 that the Russian president had probably approved the operation, and the European Court of Human Rights later formally held Russia responsible.

n: WikiLeaks publishes a quarter million diplomatic cables
ctx: The whistleblower site WikiLeaks had already published leaked military documents on the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan earlier that year, after receiving hundreds of thousands of classified files from a US Army intelligence analyst.
fa: WikiLeaks published over 250,000 confidential State Department cables in partnership with major newspapers worldwide, exposing blunt private assessments of foreign leaders and revealing details like Saudi Arabia privately urging the US to attack Iran. The leak strained American relations with dozens of governments at once.

n: The capture of the USS Pueblo
ctx: The Pueblo was a lightly armed US Navy intelligence-gathering ship operating off the coast of North Korea during a tense period of the Cold War, just before the Tet Offensive escalated the Vietnam War.
fa: North Korean patrol boats opened fire on the Pueblo and forced its surrender in what the US maintained were international waters. Its 82 surviving crew members were held and reportedly tortured for 11 months before release, while North Korea kept the ship itself as a war trophy still on display today.

ctx: Japan and the United States were not at war, but Japanese forces were in the middle of a brutal assault on the Chinese capital of Nanking, an event that would become known for its atrocities against civilians.
fa: Japanese aircraft bombed and sank the clearly marked American gunboat USS Panay as it evacuated civilians on the Yangtze River, killing three. Japan quickly apologized and paid compensation to avoid war, but the attack hardened American public opinion against Japan years before Pearl Harbor.

ctx: Relations between the two former allies had soured after the United States signed a trade treaty with Britain, which France saw as a betrayal, and French ships had begun seizing American merchant vessels in retaliation.
fa: French intermediaries demanded a personal bribe for the foreign minister and a loan to France before they would even begin peace talks with American envoys. When Congress published the demands using the code names X, Y, and Z for the French agents, the scandal triggered a wave of anti-French sentiment and an undeclared naval war.

ctx: Congo had gained independence from Belgium only months earlier, and its first elected prime minister was seen by Western governments as dangerously sympathetic to the Soviet Union during the Cold War scramble for influence in newly independent Africa.
fa: Lumumba was captured, beaten, and executed by a firing squad under Belgian officers serving a breakaway Congolese faction. A later Belgian government inquiry admitted moral responsibility, while CIA officers were separately found to have been in direct contact with his captors on the night he was killed.

n: Britain's pretext for the Opium War
ctx: British merchants had spent decades illegally smuggling opium grown in India into China against imperial law, creating widespread addiction that the Chinese government was determined to stop.
fa: When a Chinese official seized and destroyed over 20,000 chests of British opium, Britain treated the loss of the smugglers' illegal cargo as an attack on its subjects and went to war, ultimately forcing China to cede Hong Kong and open its ports on British terms.

ctx: An anti-foreign, anti-Christian uprising in China had besieged foreign legations in Beijing for 55 days before a coalition of foreign armies marched in to crush it.
fa: The victorious powers imposed a protocol forcing China to execute officials, pay an indemnity equivalent to roughly six billion dollars today spread over 39 years, and allow foreign troops to be permanently stationed on Chinese soil, terms still cited today as a symbol of China's historic humiliation by foreign powers.

ctx: Japan already controlled a strip of Manchurian territory through its South Manchuria Railway company and had long sought a pretext to seize the resource-rich region outright.
fa: Japanese army officers secretly planted a small explosive charge on their own railway line and blamed it on Chinese saboteurs, using the staged attack to justify a full invasion of Manchuria. Japan's subsequent withdrawal from the League of Nations, after the world refused to recognize the puppet state it created, was a major step toward World War II.

ctx: Hitler had already decided to invade Poland and wanted a pretext to present the coming war as a defensive response to Polish aggression, both to the German public and to the international community.
fa: SS operatives disguised as Polish soldiers staged an attack on a German radio station, even dressing a murdered prisoner in a Polish uniform as fake evidence. German radio broadcast the propaganda immediately, and Hitler cited it in his speech announcing the invasion of Poland the next morning.

ctx: Britain still maintained a colonial-era naval presence on China's rivers to protect its diplomatic and commercial interests, a practice dating back nearly a century, just as Communist forces were completing their victory in the Chinese Civil War.
fa: Communist artillery opened fire on the British frigate HMS Amethyst as it sailed the Yangtze, killing its captain and running it aground. Trapped for over three months despite failed rescue attempts, the ship finally made a daring nighttime dash to freedom, an episode widely seen as marking the end of Western gunboat privileges in China.

ctx: Iceland's economy depended overwhelmingly on its fishing industry, and it repeatedly expanded its claimed fishing waters to protect dwindling cod stocks from foreign trawlers, especially British ones.
fa: Over three separate rounds of confrontation, Icelandic patrol boats cut the nets of British trawlers while both countries' warships shadowed each other at sea. Iceland even briefly severed diplomatic relations with Britain during the final round, and Britain eventually backed down each time, accepting Iceland's claim to a 200-mile fishing zone.

ctx: Palestinian militants had hijacked an Italian cruise ship and murdered a disabled American passenger before Egypt negotiated their surrender and attempted to fly them to safety out of the country.
fa: US Navy fighter jets intercepted the Egyptian airliner carrying the hijackers mid-flight and forced it to land in Sicily, but Italy then refused American demands to hand over the plot's mastermind and let him leave the country instead, straining relations between the two allies for years.

n: The Bay of Pigs invasion and its denial
ctx: The CIA had been training Cuban exiles for over a year to invade the island and overthrow Fidel Castro, under a program explicitly designed so the United States government could deny any involvement.
fa: When the invasion collapsed within three days, Cuba immediately called an emergency United Nations meeting where American diplomats publicly denied any US role, even as evidence of CIA planning and support became clear to the world almost immediately.

ctx: Skripal was a former Russian military intelligence officer who had been convicted of spying for Britain, then released to the UK in a spy swap years before the attack.
fa: Skripal and his daughter were found unconscious on a public bench after Russian military agents smeared a military-grade nerve agent on his front door handle. A British woman who later found the discarded poison container died from exposure months afterward, and the UK expelled dozens of Russian diplomats in response.

ctx: Khashoggi was a prominent Saudi journalist living in self-imposed exile in the United States, writing columns critical of the Saudi crown prince, when he visited his own country's consulate to collect paperwork for his upcoming wedding.
fa: A 15-member Saudi squad ambushed and strangled Khashoggi inside the consulate, dismembering his body, which has never been found. Turkey had the building under surveillance and later released details from a recording, and US intelligence concluded the crown prince had probably ordered the killing.

n: Meng Wanzhou and the two Michaels
ctx: The United States had requested Meng's arrest and extradition from Canada over fraud allegations tied to Huawei's dealings with Iran, at the height of a broader trade and technology standoff between Washington and Beijing.
fa: Days after Canada arrested Huawei's chief financial officer, China detained two Canadian citizens on vague national security charges. All three were released within hours of each other three years later, once Meng struck a deal with US prosecutors, an outcome widely described as a prisoner swap in all but name.

ctx: A Panamanian law firm had spent decades quietly setting up anonymous shell companies for wealthy and powerful clients around the world seeking to hide assets from tax authorities and the public.
fa: An anonymous source leaked 11.5 million internal documents from the firm to journalists, exposing the hidden offshore holdings of a dozen sitting or former heads of state and close associates of Russia's president. The fallout forced Iceland's prime minister to resign within days.

n: Belarus forces down a passenger jet to arrest a journalist
ctx: Belarusian strongman Alexander Lukashenko was cracking down hard on his political opposition after a disputed election the previous year, and a young journalist who ran an opposition news channel happened to be on a flight passing through Belarusian airspace between two EU countries.
fa: Belarus scrambled a fighter jet to force down the passenger plane using a fabricated bomb threat as a pretext to arrest the journalist on board. The European Union responded by banning Belarusian airlines from its skies.

n: France recalls its ambassadors over the AUKUS submarine deal
ctx: Australia had signed a multi-billion-dollar contract for French conventional submarines years earlier, while secretly negotiating a rival nuclear-powered submarine deal with the US and UK behind France's back.
fa: France recalled its ambassadors from Washington and Canberra for the first time in the history of either relationship after learning of the scrapped submarine contract from a press release rather than from its allies directly, calling it a stab in the back.

ctx: A high-altitude balloon believed to be gathering intelligence drifted across sensitive US military sites for days, forcing the American government to weigh the diplomatic and safety costs of how and where to respond.
fa: US fighter jets shot the balloon down over the Atlantic once it cleared populated areas, and China protested the move as an overreaction while insisting the balloon was just a civilian weather device that had blown off course.

n: The killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar
ctx: Nijjar was a Canadian citizen and prominent advocate for an independent Sikh homeland whom India had publicly labeled a terrorist, in a diaspora community India has long accused of harboring separatist extremism.
fa: Canada's prime minister told parliament his government had credible intelligence linking Indian government agents to Nijjar's assassination outside a Sikh temple in Vancouver. Both countries expelled each other's diplomats, and India froze visa services for Canadians for weeks.

ctx: Warmbier was a 21-year-old American student on a guided tour of North Korea, one of the few ways foreigners could legally visit the isolated country, when he was accused of taking a propaganda poster from his hotel wall.
fa: North Korea sentenced Warmbier to 15 years of hard labor, and he fell into a coma in custody under circumstances Pyongyang never adequately explained. He was flown home unconscious after 17 months and died days later, hardening American policy toward North Korea for years.

ctx: Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 was a scheduled civilian passenger flight from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur that crossed over eastern Ukraine, a region where fighting had broken out earlier that year between Ukrainian forces and Russian-backed separatists.
fa: All 298 people aboard were killed when the plane was struck by a missile over separatist-held territory. A multinational Joint Investigation Team led by Dutch prosecutors spent years piecing together phone intercepts, satellite imagery, and physical evidence to conclude the missile came from a Russian military unit, a finding Russia has consistently denied.
